Dive in, second design

One sheet, three things, nothing new to read. Every row, heading, marked word, place, coastline and route leg on this page is what the shipped data draws for these two verses; nothing is hand-placed except the sea label. Generated by scripts/export-dive-in.mjs.

1 · The entrance

One line under the chosen verse, and it is real content. The strongest passage, with the words the two verses share already marked, and how many more there are. A journey chapter leads with the route instead. A verse with nothing beneath shows nothing. Tap the line in the first phone: the sheet rises exactly as the shipped one does, and the chapter stays where it was.

2 · The view

Verse held, the passages that pick it up, where it happens. The map is the parchment relief you chose (treatment a: the shipped hillshade under a hypsometric ramp, clipped to the coast polygons), framed tight on the chapter, with labels sized to the frame. A row is the reference, the BSB heading it sits under in grey, and two lines of the passage with the shared words marked. No author, no relation words: the marks say "quotes" and "names Damascus too" without saying it, and they make no claim about direction. The map is the chapter's own places on parchment, with a bearing or two kept faint so the reader is never lost.

2b · Follow, and come back

Two depths, one tap each. Tap a row and it opens in place: the whole passage, marks kept, nothing else moves. That answers most curiosity without leaving the verse. The open row offers one more step, "Read it in James 2", which puts the chapter itself in the sheet with the passage lit and a Back that returns to exactly this view. Both are live in these phones.

3 · The journey

One leg at a time, with its verse. The whole route stays faint; one leg is lit, with the only arrowhead on the map. The strip of stops under the map is the control: tap a stop and the leg that reaches it lights; the strip shows the journey's shape, silent stretch dotted. The caption keeps a fixed height across steps (two lines of verse, the places marked); tap the verse to read it whole, the same gesture as a row. The map itself is a live viewport: drag to pan, pinch or wheel to zoom, plus quiet zoom buttons and a recentre mark that appears only once you have moved. No full-screen page; the card is the map. Stepping: tap a stop, use the chevrons, or swipe the caption. On the strip the past is ink, the present is accent, the future a hairline. Motion: each segment of the strip changes state where it stands, settling one after another in the direction of travel on a jump; the lit leg draws itself over 950 ms and the arrowhead lands last; the caption is a carousel and slides sideways with the step; rows open in place by growing, and the chapter slides in beside the view and back again. All of it on the app's own tokens, none of it under reduced motion. No numbers, no gradient, no list: a route that doubles back is no harder than one that does not, because only one leg is ever lit. Every leg is a solid line; the silent fourteen years read as such in the caption, which carries the note the data holds, not as a different kind of line.

4 · Desktop

The same sheet as a panel beside the text. The entrance line is identical.

5 · Bounded by the data

The gate. Galatians 1:17's strongest connection scores 4 against a line of 30, so the live app shows no connections there at all. This design opens the door when the top passage is a parallel account: it names a place this chapter names (Acts 9 names Damascus and Jerusalem). That is measured on the shipped place list, not guessed. Rows below show each connection with its score, the words shared, and the places shared.

What this drops from the first design.

  • The context-line classifier and the 66-book "who" table. The marks carry the relation; the reference carries the who.
  • The glimpse strip. Replaced by one line of real content with a count.
  • The verse-opens transition. The chapter never leaves; the shipped sheet motion stays.
  • Numbers, visit pairs, gradient, draw-in and the step list. Replaced by one lit leg and its verse.
  • The sea band. Coastlines are clipped as polygons, so the fill closes along the frame edge instead of a chord across the land.
  • Region stops that sit on a city. OpenBible places "Syria" on Damascus and "Judea" on Jerusalem; a region stop at a city's exact point is drawn as a label on the next leg, never as a return to the city.
